prompt: A team already knows Docker Compose well and wants its `compose.yaml` to run across three machines with the least new to learn. Which tool fits that wish most directly?
hint: One of them reads the same file.

choices.text: Nomad, because it is one binary
choices.why: One binary is easy to install, but its jobs are written in HCL, not in a `compose.yaml`.

choices.text: Swarm mode, with `docker stack deploy`
choices.why: Right. Swarm is built into the Docker Engine and deploys a compose file as it is.

choices.text: ECS, because AWS runs its control plane
choices.why: ECS takes task definitions in its own format; the compose file would have to be rewritten.

choices.text: A managed Kubernetes, since the provider handles everything
choices.why: The provider runs the control plane, and the team still has to learn the objects of lesson 2.

prompt: A company has many Java programs and a few virtual machines that were never put in an image, and wants one scheduler for all of them. Which of the four is built for that mix?
hint: Only one of them schedules things that are not containers.

choices.text: Swarm mode
choices.why: Swarm runs containers and nothing else.

choices.text: A platform such as Heroku
choices.why: A platform takes an image or source code, never a virtual machine you already have.

choices.text: Nomad
choices.why: Right. Its jobs can be containers, plain executables, Java programs or virtual machines.

choices.text: ECS on Fargate
choices.why: Fargate runs tasks made of containers; the programs would have to be packaged first.

prompt: What is the main price a team pays for ECS's convenience, compared with Kubernetes?
hint: Think about the day the team wants to leave.

choices.text: A fee for every hour its control plane runs
choices.why: AWS does not charge for the ECS control plane; you pay for the machines or Fargate.

choices.text: Its task definitions mean something only on AWS
choices.why: Right. Moving to another provider means rewriting the descriptions, where Kubernetes objects travel.

choices.text: It cannot run more than one copy of a container
choices.why: A service says how many tasks to run, and runs them behind a load balancer.

choices.text: Its licence changed and restricts competing services
choices.why: That is Nomad's 2023 change; ECS is a service, not software you license.

prompt: Match each tool with what you describe to it.
hint: The middle column of the table.

pairs.right: Tasks and services in AWS's format

right_distractors: Nothing at all: it reads the running containers

prompt: Kubernetes releases three minor versions a year and supports each for about fourteen months. What does that mean for a cluster nobody upgrades?
hint: Fourteen months is the whole window.

choices.text: It stays supported as long as it keeps running
choices.why: Support is attached to a version, and a version's window ends whether the cluster runs or not.

choices.text: It stops working on the day support ends
choices.why: It keeps running; it stops receiving fixes, which is the danger.

choices.text: It falls out of support within about a year and a half
choices.why: Right. Upgrades are recurring work that comes with the cluster.

choices.text: It is upgraded automatically by the next release
choices.why: Nothing upgrades your own cluster for you; a managed provider may, on its schedule.

prompt: Three engineers run one public API on one cloud, deploy twice a week, and see steady traffic. They are asked to move it to Kubernetes 'to be ready for growth'. What does this lesson suggest?
hint: Count how many of the table's questions point towards Kubernetes today.

choices.text: Stay with that cloud's own runner until the questions change
choices.why: Right. One service, steady load, rare deploys and nobody to operate a cluster all point the other way.

choices.text: Move now, because a cluster is cheaper the earlier it starts
choices.why: The cluster's costs start the day it exists, and here they would buy little.

choices.text: Move to Swarm mode, because it is always the smaller step
choices.why: Swarm is still machines and a manager to run; the cloud's runner asks for less.

choices.text: Move to Nomad, which has no control plane
choices.why: Nomad's servers are its control plane; somebody runs them.

prompt: Which of these are costs of Kubernetes that are not money? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section lists four parts of the bill.

choices.text: Keeping the control plane up
choices.why: Right: if it stops, nothing can change.

choices.text: Upgrading on the project's schedule
choices.why: Right: three minor versions a year.

choices.text: Rewriting the compose file for every deploy
choices.why: A cluster reads its own objects; nobody rewrites a compose file per deploy.

choices.text: Learning a vocabulary of objects
choices.why: Right: and everyone who touches the cluster needs some of it.

choices.text: Losing the ability to run more than one service
choices.why: It is the opposite; many services is where a cluster pays for itself.

prompt: Going down the comparison table, from your own Kubernetes to a platform, what changes together?
hint: Two columns move in the same direction.

choices.text: You pay less and control more
choices.why: Control goes down the table, and a platform's rate is higher than the machines.

choices.text: You operate less and your files travel less
choices.why: Right. That trade is the pattern; Kubernetes is unusual in sitting at both ends of it.

choices.text: The files stay the same and only the price changes
choices.why: The format changes too: compose, HCL, task definitions, an image and a size.

choices.text: Each step adds a control plane you run
choices.why: It is the reverse: lower down, the provider runs it.
